content.title: About
content.content: Arugula (Eruca vesicaria) is a salad green in the cabbage family with a peppery, slightly nutty flavor. The leaves are tender and elongated with toothed edges. Arugula is eaten fresh in salads, put on pizza, and added to pasta, sandwiches, sauces, and pesto.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Arugula is related to cabbage, mustard, radish, and wasabi.
The name arugula is Italian-derived; in the United Kingdom it is called rocket.
Arugula is especially popular in Italian and Mediterranean cooking, where it is put on pizza after baking.
Young leaves are milder, while older ones are sharper and more bitter.
Arugula flowers are also edible.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K plays a role in blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: The body partly converts carotenoids into vitamin A.

items.title: Contains vitamin C and folate
items.content: These nutrients support the immune system and cell formation.

items.title: Contains natural nitrates
items.content: Nitrates from vegetables are studied in relation to vascular health.

items.title: Contains glucosinolates
items.content: As in other cruciferous vegetables, these compounds turn into isothiocyanates and are studied as antioxidants.

items.title: Vitamin K and blood thinners
items.content: People taking warfarin and other anticoagulants should not suddenly change how much of these greens they eat without consulting a doctor.

items.title: Thyroid
items.content: A large amount of raw cruciferous vegetables may affect the thyroid in people with iodine deficiency.

items.title: Pungency
items.content: The sharp taste can irritate a sensitive stomach.

items.title: Safety
items.content: Greens should be washed thoroughly, including ready-to-eat packaged ones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat arugula fresh: put it in salads, on pizza after baking, in sandwiches, pasta, and risotto, or make it into pesto. Its tender leaves should not be heated for long. It pairs well with cheese, tomatoes, pear, nuts, and balsamic vinegar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store arugula in the refrigerator in a container or bag with a paper towel for three to five days. Do not wash the leaves in advance, and rinse them thoroughly before eating.

beef-stew-with-potatoes-puerto-rican-sty.title: Beef Stew with Potatoes, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Beef stew with potatoes Puerto Rican style is a classic island dish where beef is slowly braised with aromatic spices, tomato sauce, olive oil, olives, capers, and chunks of potato. The stew has a rich, slightly sweet flavor with hints of garlic, oregano, and vinegar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Puerto Rico the stew is often cooked in clay pots (cazuelas), which impart a unique earthy aroma.
Traditional recipes include a “adobo” blend of vinegar, garlic, oregano, and olive oil.
Potatoes are cut into large cubes so they hold their shape and absorb the sauce.
The dish is commonly served with rice, beans, and fried plantains.
Locally it is known as “Carne Guisada” and is a staple for holidays and family gatherings.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Red meat supplies easily absorbed iron and zinc, supporting immunity and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The stew delivers B12, B6, and niacin, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Potassium from potatoes
items.content: Potatoes add potassium, which helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Garlic, oregano, and vinegar contain antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Beef can be high in saturated fat; choose lean cuts if you have cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Salt and sauce
items.content: The stew often contains added salt and soy‑based sauces, which may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to garlic, oregano, or olives.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of meat, oil, and potatoes, the dish is calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot, typically alongside white rice, beans, or fried plantains. A squeeze of lime or fresh cilantro adds brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, portion into freezer‑safe containers and freeze up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken skin is the edible outer covering of the bird, surrounding the body and wings. When cooked properly it becomes crispy, aromatic, and has a rich meaty flavor. It is commonly used for frying, roasting, and adding depth to broths.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken skin contains more fat than the meat, but a portion of this fat consists of beneficial monounsaturated and polyunsaturated acids.
In many traditional cuisines (e.g., Chinese, Mexican, and South American) crispy skin is considered a delicacy.
During frying the skin releases aromatic compounds that enhance the flavor of the whole dish.
Chicken skin can be used to make gelatinous stocks, sauces, and soups, providing body and taste.

items.title: Collagen source
items.content: The skin is rich in collagen, which supports skin, joint, and connective‑tissue health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It provides B2 (riboflavin) and B3 (niacin), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fatty acids
items.content: Some of the fats are monounsaturated, which can be heart‑friendly when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken skin contains zinc and iron, essential for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Chicken skin is calorie‑dense; excessive intake may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: It contains a notable amount of cholesterol, which can be a concern for people with elevated blood lipids.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins found in the skin.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improperly handled skin can harbor bacteria such as Salmonella; thorough cooking is required.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken skin can be fried until golden, baked in the oven, added to soups and stocks for richness, or used as a crunchy garnish for salads. Before cooking, excess fat can be trimmed if a lower‑calorie option is desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh skin in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 2‑3 days. Frozen skin keeps well for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, made with cooking spray

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of eggs beaten with cheese and cooked using cooking spray instead of butter or oil. It cooks quickly, provides protein, calcium, and a modest amount of fat thanks to the spray.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cooking spray allows cooking with minimal added fat while preserving flavor.
Cheese adds not only taste but also extra calcium and protein.
The dish has been popular in the US since the early 1980s as a quick breakfast or snack.
Different cheeses (cheddar, mozzarella, feta) give varied flavor profiles.
Eggs are a rich source of vitamin D and choline.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low added fat
items.content: Using cooking spray reduces added oil, making the meal less calorie-dense.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs provide B12, riboflavin, and folate, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Choline for brain health
items.content: Choline in eggs supports brain function and memory.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs or cheese.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Certain cheeses can be high in sodium, increasing overall salt intake.

items.title: Quality of cooking spray
items.content: Sprays containing propellants may be undesirable for sensitive individuals; choose additive‑free options.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat eggs with grated cheese, season with salt and pepper. Heat a skillet, spray with cooking spray, pour the mixture, and stir‑cook until the desired consistency is reached.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed mushrooms are edible fungi, usually button mushrooms or oyster mushrooms, filled with a mixture of cheese, meat, vegetables, or spices. They are often served as an appetizer or side dish and are popular in European and Asian cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms readily absorb the flavors of the stuffing, making each bite unique.
Stuffed mushrooms are commonly baked, which preserves their juiciness and aroma.
In countries such as Italy, stuffed mushrooms are a traditional holiday dish.
Mushrooms are rich in B‑vitamins and minerals like selenium and potassium.
When properly prepared, stuffed mushrooms can be kept in the fridge for up to 3 days.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms provide niacin, riboflavin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Stuffed mushrooms give a feeling of fullness with relatively few calories, helpful for weight management.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports immune health.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium in mushrooms helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Stuffings often contain salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Potential toxins
items.content: Raw or improperly cooked wild mushrooms can contain toxins; only use verified species.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some stuffing recipes include preservatives or artificial flavorings that may not suit everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stuffed mushrooms can be served hot as an appetizer, added to salads, pasta, or rice dishes. They reheat well in the microwave or oven until the tops are golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared stuffed mushrooms in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in bags at –18 °C; fully reheat before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Sour cream is a fermented dairy product made by culturing cream with lactic acid bacteria. Regular sour cream has a smooth, creamy texture, a mildly tangy flavor, and is commonly used in Russian and Eastern European cuisine as a topping, dip, or ingredient for sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional sour cream is produced from cream with a fat content of 30 % or higher.
In Russia, sour cream is considered a staple and is often served with pancakes, dumplings, and borscht.
Sour cream is available in various fat levels, from 10 % (light) to 40 % (extra‑rich).
The bacterial cultures used create probiotic benefits and give the product its characteristic tang.
It stays fresh longest when kept refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Sour cream provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B2 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Offers a modest amount of high‑quality dairy protein.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: The live cultures may help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Short‑chain fatty acids
items.content: Its fat includes short‑chain fatty acids that are easily digested.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Sour cream contains lactose, which can cause discomfort for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to sour cream.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Full‑fat sour cream is calorie‑dense, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Once opened, the product loses freshness quickly; proper storage is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use sour cream as a topping for salads, in dips, in baked dishes, soups, and potato recipes. It can be folded into pancake batter, added to casseroles, or mixed into sauces such as a classic sour‑cream dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sour cream in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in its original container or a sealed jar. After opening, consume within 5–7 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may separate.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy milk is a plant-based drink made from soybeans: they are soaked, ground with water, and strained. It has a mild, slightly beany flavor and a creamy texture. Soy milk is drunk, added to coffee, porridge, baked goods, and smoothies, and is also used to make tofu.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy milk has been drunk in China for many centuries.
Tofu is made from soy milk by curdling it, in the same way as cheese.
When soy milk is heated, a skin forms on the surface, which is made into yuba in Asian cooking.
Of the plant-based milks, soy is closest to cow milk in protein content.
Many soy milks are fortified with calcium, vitamin D, and B12.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Soy milk provides protein and suits plant-based diets.

items.title: Lactose- and cholesterol-free
items.content: It contains no lactose or cholesterol, so it suits people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Contains unsaturated fats
items.content: Most of its fat is unsaturated.

items.title: May be fortified
items.content: Fortified soy milk provides calcium, vitamin D, and B12.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Soy isoflavones are plant compounds that are actively studied.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy is a common allergen, so people with this allergy should avoid soy milk.

items.title: Thyroid and medications
items.content: Soy may reduce the absorption of thyroid medication; people with thyroid conditions should discuss such foods with a doctor.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Flavored and sweetened soy milk can contain a lot of sugar.

items.title: For infants
items.content: Soy milk is not a substitute for breast milk or infant formula; it should not be given to children under one year old.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink soy milk chilled, add it to coffee, tea, porridge, smoothies, and baked goods, and make sauces and desserts with it. Shake the carton before use. Homemade soy milk must always be boiled for about 15–20 minutes, because raw soy contains compounds that interfere with digestion.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened long-life cartons in a cool place. After opening, store soy milk in the refrigerator and use it within a few days. Keep homemade soy milk in the refrigerator for two to three days. Discard milk that smells sour.

content.title: About
content.content: A whole grain waffle is a crisp, airy product made from whole grain flour, water, eggs, and a small amount of vegetable oil. Using the whole grain retains more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals compared with regular white‑flour waffles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain waffles are often prepared with a blend of wheat and oat flours, boosting their nutritional profile.
Traditionally waffles are cooked in patterned irons that create the characteristic grid.
Waffles can be sweet or savory, depending on add‑ins such as berries, nuts, or cheese.
They are a popular quick breakfast or snack, especially in Northern European countries.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grain flour keeps the bran and germ, increasing fiber content which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Waffles provide thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: They supply iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, important for bones and muscles.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact than refined flour
items.content: Whole grain products raise blood sugar more slowly, aiding weight management.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: Waffles deliver a modest amount of plant‑based protein that can complement the diet.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Waffles made with wheat whole grain flour contain gluten and may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Added sugar in some recipes
items.content: Sweetened versions can contain added sugars, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite the whole grain base, waffles are still relatively calorie‑dense due to oil and eggs; portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve waffles warm, drizzled with honey, fruit sauce, or yogurt. They also work as a base for sandwiches with ham, cheese, or vegetables. For a healthier option, top with fresh fruit and nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep waffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑top bag – they retain flavor and texture for up to 2 months. Reheat in a toaster or microwave before serving.
